sections.name: General Knowledge / Current Affairs of India and Goa

p1.title: Passage 1
paras: Much of what we do each day is not decided at all. We take the same route to work, reach for the same seat at the table and accept the settings that came with a new phone, not because we have weighed the alternatives but because the choice was made once and has since been running on its own. Psychologists describe such behaviour as habitual, and they have found that it is triggered less by intention than by context: the place, the time and the preceding action cue the response before any deliberate thought occurs.

This finding has an uncomfortable implication for anyone who hopes to change by willpower alone. Resolving to eat less or to read more is a matter of intention, but the old habit is tied to the old context, and so it reasserts itself as soon as attention lapses. People who succeed in changing their behaviour tend instead to alter their surroundings. They keep the biscuit tin out of sight, place the book on the pillow, or attach the new action to an existing routine, so that one cue now leads to a different response. Seen in this light, a habit is neither a vice nor a virtue in itself; it is an economy of the mind, freeing attention for matters that genuinely need it. The task is not to abolish habits but to arrange for good ones.

p2.title: Passage 2
paras: The migrant who arrives in a city with a bundle of belongings and the address of a relative is often treated in official discourse as a problem to be managed. Yet the city could scarcely function without him. He builds its towers, cooks in its kitchens, drives its delivery vehicles and cleans its offices before the offices open. What the city is reluctant to provide is a place for him to live. Formal housing is priced far beyond his wages, and so he settles where land is unclaimed or uncertain: beside railway lines, along drains, on slopes too steep for developers. These settlements are routinely described as encroachments, a word that places the fault entirely on those who occupy them.

A more honest account would acknowledge that informal housing is the market's answer to a demand that planning has refused to anticipate. Periodic demolitions do not remove the need; they merely displace it to the next vacant patch, destroying savings and schooling along the way. Cities that have managed migration better have done so by securing tenure for existing residents, extending water and sanitation to settlements before regularising them, and setting aside land for low-cost rental housing near places of work. None of this is charity. It is the ordinary infrastructure of a city that wishes to keep the workers on whom it depends.

questions.q: Which is the most suitable title for the passage?
questions.why: Main idea: habits are cued by context, so successful change comes from altering surroundings.

questions.q: According to psychologists, habitual behaviour is triggered mainly by:
opts: The place, the time and the preceding action.
The strength of a person's willpower.
The advice of friends and family.
questions.why: Detail: 'triggered less by intention than by context: the place, the time and the preceding action'.

questions.q: A person who resolves to exercise every morning but changes nothing else in his routine is, according to the passage, most likely to:
opts: Find the old routine returning as soon as his attention slips.
Find that exercise becomes automatic at once.
Lose all his other habits as well.
Succeed, since intention controls habitual behaviour.
questions.why: Inference: 'the old habit is tied to the old context, and so it reasserts itself as soon as attention lapses'.

questions.q: The examples of the biscuit tin and the book on the pillow are given to show that:
opts: Successful changers reshape their surroundings to support new behaviour.
Reading in bed is a harmful habit.
Willpower alone is enough to change behaviour.
Certain foods should be avoided at night.
questions.why: Purpose: they follow 'People who succeed in changing their behaviour tend instead to alter their surroundings'.

questions.q: In the phrase "an economy of the mind", the word "economy" most nearly means:
opts: A system of trade and money
questions.why: Vocabulary: a habit is an economy because it is 'freeing attention for matters that genuinely need it'.

questions.q: Which of the following best captures the main argument of the passage?
opts: Informal settlements should be cleared to make way for formal housing.
Migrants are a burden that cities must manage through stricter controls.
Cities depend on migrant workers but fail to house them, and should plan for their housing rather than demolish settlements.
Migrants should return to villages where housing is cheaper.
questions.why: Main idea: 'the city could scarcely function without him', yet it is 'reluctant to provide... a place for him to live'; the author proposes tenure, services and rental housing.

questions.q: According to the passage, where do migrants usually settle?
opts: On unclaimed or uncertain land such as beside railway lines and along drains.
In rental flats near the city centre.
In formal housing provided by their employers.
In villages on the outskirts, commuting daily.
questions.why: Detail: 'he settles where land is unclaimed or uncertain: beside railway lines, along drains, on slopes too steep for developers'.

questions.q: The author's remark about the word 'encroachments' suggests that the term:
opts: is the word migrants themselves prefer.
is legally precise and therefore fair.
unfairly blames residents while ignoring the failure of planning.
justifies the periodic demolition of settlements.
questions.why: Inference: the word 'places the fault entirely on those who occupy them', whereas the author says planning 'refused to anticipate' the demand.

questions.q: The author's purpose in stating 'None of this is charity' is to:
opts: present housing for migrants as practical self-interest of the city rather than benevolence.
reject all public spending on housing.
argue that migrants should pay the full cost of services.
criticise charitable organisations working in settlements.
questions.why: Purpose: the next sentence calls these measures 'the ordinary infrastructure of a city that wishes to keep the workers on whom it depends'.

questions.q: As used in the passage, 'tenure' means:
opts: the legal right to occupy land or housing
a period of holding an official post
a fee charged for rented housing
questions.why: Vocabulary: 'securing tenure for existing residents' means guaranteeing their right to stay where they live.

questions.q: Choose the correct modal: “____ you please lend me your pen?”
questions.why: 'Could' is used for a polite request. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Choose the correct article: “Honesty is ____ best policy.”
questions.why: Fixed proverb: 'the best policy'. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Choose the word opposite in meaning to “benign”:
questions.why: 'Benign' means gentle or harmless; 'malignant' means harmful or evil in intent. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Find the correctly spelt word:
questions.why: Double l and double n. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Choose the correct word: “The committee needs a ____ arbiter who has no stake in the outcome.”
questions.why: 'Disinterested' means impartial; 'uninterested' means bored. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: On which date is International Mountain Day observed?
questions.why: UN observance on 11 December each year. Dec.

questions.q: On which date is World Rabies Day observed?
questions.why: Marks the death anniversary of Louis Pasteur, who made the first rabies vaccine. Sep 2026.

questions.q: Dr B. R. Ambedkar called which Article the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution?
questions.why: Article 32 gives the right to constitutional remedies.

questions.q: Who took charge as the 47th Director General of Armed Forces Medical Services (DGAFMS) in September 2026?
opts: Air Marshal K. A. A. Sanjeeb
questions.why: He succeeded Surgeon Vice Admiral Arti Sarin. Sep 2026.

questions.q: Who was elected the first President of the Indian UniSport Federation in October 2026?
questions.why: Samanta is the founder of KIIT and KISS in Bhubaneswar. Oct 2026.

questions.q: ISRO's EOS-05 (GISAT-1A), launched on 4 September 2026, was carried by:
questions.why: ISRO's return to flight after the PSLV-C62 failure of January 2026. Sep 2026.

questions.q: Astrophysicist Annapurni Subramaniam became the first Indian woman to receive which medal, at the COSPAR Scientific Assembly in Florence?
questions.why: The medal is given jointly by COSPAR and ISRO. Aug 2026.

questions.q: Sauj Jheel, declared a Ramsar site along with Sukhna Wetland in October 2026, is located in:
questions.why: Sukhna Wetland is in Chandigarh; Sauj Jheel is known for Sarus cranes. Oct 2026.

questions.q: Who became France's first men's singles world champion in badminton, at the BWF World Championships 2026 in New Delhi?
questions.why: Lanier beat Japan's Kodai Naraoka 21-11, 21-11 in the final. Aug 2026.

questions.q: INS Tarkash represented India at IBSAMAR IX, the India–Brazil–South Africa maritime exercise. Where was it held?
questions.why: The ninth edition ended on 20 October. Oct 2026.

questions.q: Suresh is the father of Vijay. Vijay is the son of Pooja. Pooja is the wife of Suresh. How is Pooja related to Vijay?
questions.why: Draw the family tree from the statements; the answer is Mother. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Statements: Some remedies are tablets. No tablets are liquids. Conclusions: I. No remedies are liquids. II. Some remedies are not liquids.
questions.why: Checked against every possible diagram of the statements: I need not be true, II must be true. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Find the wrong number in the series: 39, 45, 51, 54, 63, 69, 75
questions.why: In the correct series each term adds 6, so 54 should be 57. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: In how many different ways can the letters of the word PEPPER be arranged?
questions.why: 6 letters with repeats: 6! ÷ 3! ÷ 2! = 60. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 6:10?
questions.why: Angle = |30×6 − 5.5×10| = 125°. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Ravi walks 2 m North, then turns right and walks 5 m, then turns right and walks 2 m. Which direction is Ravi facing now?
questions.why: Follow each turn from the first direction: the last leg is towards the South. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: What is the angle between the hands of a clock at 4:10?
questions.why: Angle = |30×4 − 5.5×10| = 65°. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Find the wrong number in the series: 34, 41, 55, 76, 104, 136, 181
questions.why: In the correct series the differences increase by 7 each time, so 136 should be 139. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: If 28 June 2026 was a Sunday, what day of the week was 20 February 2027?
questions.why: 237 days later; 237 mod 7 = 6, so count 6 days on from Sunday. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: If TABLET is written as UCEPJZ in a certain code, how is NURSING written in that code?
questions.why: In the code the 1st letter moves 1 place, the 2nd 2 places, the 3rd 3 places, and so on: NURSING → OWUWNTN. GPSC-style practice item.

questions.q: Suspicion, secretiveness, jealousy and fixed ideas are the mental features of which miasm?
questions.why: Sycotic mentals are suspicious, secretive, jealous and fixed in ideas; psora is anxious and fearful, syphilis destructive and depressed.

questions.q: A slight aggravation in the first hours after a well-chosen remedy in an acute disease is, according to §§157 and 158:
opts: a good sign that the disease will probably yield to the first dose
a sign that the remedy was wrong and must be antidoted
a sign that the dose should be repeated at once
a sign that the case is incurable
questions.why: §158: the slight homoeopathic aggravation in the first hours is a very good prognostic that the acute disease will yield to the first dose.

questions.q: According to §215, almost all so-called mental and emotional diseases are:
opts: bodily diseases in which the mental symptoms have increased while the bodily symptoms have declined
purely spiritual diseases that need no medicine
diseases caused only by emotional shocks
local diseases of the brain substance
questions.why: §215: mental diseases are corporeal diseases in which the derangement of mind and disposition has become predominant, like a one-sided disease.

questions.q: Eruptions behind the ears and in the bends of the joints that ooze a thick, sticky, honey-like fluid, in an obese, chilly, constipated woman, call for:
questions.why: Graphites: eruptions oozing a thick, honey-like, glutinous fluid, especially behind the ears and in flexures (Allen's Keynotes).

questions.q: Pyrogenium was originally prepared from:
questions.why: Pyrogenium was made by Drysdale from lean beef left to decompose in the sun; it is used in septic fevers.

questions.q: A haughty woman to whom objects around her look small, while she feels physically large, needs:
questions.why: Platina: things look smaller than they are while she feels tall and superior (Boericke).

questions.q: The size number of a globule (for example No. 10 or No. 30) indicates:
opts: the weight in milligrams of 10 globules
the number of globules in one gram
the number of globules medicated by one drop
the length in millimetres of 10 globules placed in a row
questions.why: Globule number is the length in mm of ten globules laid side by side, so a No. 10 globule is about 1 mm across.

questions.q: Causticum (Hahnemann's 'tinctura acris sine kali') is prepared by:
opts: heating oyster shell with flowers of sulphur
distilling freshly slaked lime with a solution of potassium bisulphate
questions.why: Causticum is the distillate obtained from freshly burnt, slaked lime and a solution of bisulphate of potash.

questions.q: The rubric 'Mind, Loquacity' means:
questions.why: Loquacity is talkativeness, as in Lachesis.

questions.q: Kent's Repertory contains how many chapters?
questions.why: Kent's Repertory runs in 37 chapters, from Mind to Generalities.

questions.q: The most specific serum marker of myocardial injury is:
questions.why: Troponins are specific to heart muscle and stay raised for days; CK-MB, AST and LDH are less specific.

questions.q: The ankle jerk tests the spinal segments:
questions.why: The Achilles reflex is S1–S2; the knee jerk is L3–L4 and the biceps jerk C5–C6.

questions.q: A lesion of the primary visual cortex of one occipital lobe typically produces:
opts: total blindness of the eye on the same side
contralateral homonymous hemianopia with macular sparing
questions.why: The visual cortex receives the opposite half-field of both eyes; the macula is often spared owing to dual blood supply. Bitemporal loss is from the optic chiasma.

questions.q: The normal platelet count in adults is about:
questions.why: Normal platelets are 150,000 to 450,000/uL; 4,000 to 11,000 is the WBC range and 4.5 to 5.5 million the RBC count.

questions.q: White blood cell casts in urine are characteristic of:
questions.why: WBC casts form in the tubules and so localise inflammation to the kidney, as in pyelonephritis; cystitis gives pus cells without casts.

questions.q: A blood urea nitrogen (BUN) to creatinine ratio above 20:1 most suggests:
questions.why: In prerenal states urea is reabsorbed avidly along with water, raising BUN out of proportion to creatinine; in intrinsic renal damage the ratio is usually below 15.

questions.q: The antiviral drug used for treating influenza, including H1N1, is:
questions.why: Oseltamivir is a neuraminidase inhibitor used for influenza A and B, best within 48 hours of onset.

questions.q: Fever, sore throat, a strawberry tongue, a fine 'sandpaper' rash with circumoral pallor and Pastia's lines suggest:
questions.why: Scarlet fever, due to erythrogenic toxin of Group A streptococcus, gives this rash with accentuation in skin folds (Pastia's lines).

questions.q: A first-line oral antiviral for chronic hepatitis B is:
questions.why: Tenofovir and entecavir are potent nucleos(t)ide analogues with a high barrier to resistance used for chronic HBV.

questions.q: The pentavalent vaccine in India's UIP protects against diphtheria, pertussis, tetanus and:
opts: hepatitis B and Haemophilus influenzae type b
questions.why: Pentavalent = DPT + Hep B + Hib, given at 6, 10 and 14 weeks.

questions.q: While a woman is on magnesium sulphate, the first clinical sign of toxicity to watch for is:
questions.why: Knee jerk disappears at serum levels around 10 mEq/L, before respiratory depression; so the reflex is checked before every repeat dose.

questions.q: The commonest cause of fever in the first 24–48 hours after an abdominal operation is:
questions.why: Early postoperative fever is usually pulmonary collapse; wound infection appears around days 5–7.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT one of India's 'Big Four' venomous snakes?
questions.why: The Big Four are the spectacled cobra, common krait, Russell's viper and saw-scaled viper.

questions.q: Sharing of fees between a referring doctor and a consultant without the patient's knowledge is called:
questions.why: Fee-splitting (dichotomy) is infamous conduct; covering is shielding an unqualified person.

questions.q: In a common-source, single-exposure (point-source) epidemic, the epidemic curve typically shows:
opts: several waves separated by one serial interval each
a slow rise lasting many incubation periods
a steady level of cases over years
a sharp rise and fall, with all cases occurring within one incubation period
questions.why: A point-source outbreak (e.g. food poisoning) clusters within one incubation period with no secondary waves; propagated epidemics show gradual rise and successive waves.
